claims.text: In solidified polycrystalline FeNiCrMn, dynamic mechanical response is controlled by temperature- and strain-rate-dependent nucleation and evolution of dislocations and stacking faults.
Low temperatures and high strain rates kinetically limit thermally activated dislocation glide.
Restricted dislocation glide causes dislocation accumulation and entanglement.
Low-temperature, high-rate deformation favors the formation and retention of stacking faults.
Dislocation entanglements inhibit dislocation motion and increase yield strength.
Accumulated stacking faults and dislocation entanglements increase the work-hardening rate.
Higher temperature enhances dislocation mobility through thermal activation.
Enhanced dislocation mobility at higher temperature reduces stacking-fault buildup and dislocation entanglement.
The reduction of stacking faults and dislocation entanglement at higher temperature lowers dynamic yield strength even at high strain rate.
Higher-temperature deformation lowers dynamic strength while maintaining ductility.
Dislocations can nucleate near grain boundaries, propagate while leaving stacking faults, and become entangled near grain boundaries.
At low temperature, increasing strain rate will significantly increase yield strength and work-hardening rate.
Low-temperature, high-rate strengthening will be accompanied by increased stacking-fault fraction and dislocation density.
At elevated temperature, increasing strain rate will cause a less pronounced increase in yield strength because dislocation mobility mitigates defect accumulation.
Under quasi-static room-temperature deformation, the proposed microstructural mechanisms operate at an intermediate level.
Large grain-size variations may change the governing deformation behavior enough to place the material outside the hypothesis's applicable boundary.
FCC-to-BCC or FCC-to-HCP transformations can significantly alter the operative deformation mechanisms.
The controlled study compares tension and compression from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1 at 77 K, 300 K, and 900 K while measuring stress, hardening, dislocation density, and stacking-fault fraction.
A failure to observe the predicted defect accumulation or the corresponding strength and work-hardening changes would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions require deformation to retain the alloy's initial microstructural state, whereas the hypothesis and measurements require substantial deformation-induced nucleation, accumulation, and entanglement of dislocations and stacking faults. Retaining the initial phase is compatible with the hypothesis, but retaining the initial microstructural state is not.
